note: THE ERROR CODE REGISTRY. One row per short code that a PRODUCTION build of an Exodra
package can throw. A development build throws the full sentence instead; the code is what
survives the fold of `typeof process !== 'undefined' && process.env.NODE_ENV !==
'production' ? <prose> : 'EXO0001'`, and it is the only thing a user's console will show.
THIS FILE MUST NEVER BE IMPORTED BY A SHIPPED MODULE. Importing it would put every
explanation back into every bundle, which is the exact cost the codes exist to remove — see
`measurement` below for the only statement of that cost in this repository. It is JSON, and
`resolveJsonModule` is on in the root tsconfig, so the language would happily let a file
under packages/*/src import it and tsup would inline the whole thing into dist. Nothing
about the FORMAT prevents that. What prevents it is:
1. `packages/core/src/tests/errorCodeRegistry.test.ts` parses every file under packages/*/src
that mentions this filename at all and fails if any of them names it in an import, an
export-from, a dynamic `import()` or a `require()`. A COMMENT naming it is fine and is
what a converted site should carry — that is how the next reader finds the row. That
test runs in the normal `vitest` suite, which `release:check` runs, which CI runs. It
is the guarantee with teeth.
2. A dependency-cruiser rule, `error-registry-does-not-ship`, forbids the edge
structurally. This note used to add that nothing ran it — "nothing in `release:check`
or in any workflow under .github/ runs `graph:check` today" — and that has stopped
being true: `graph:check` is the fourth step of `release:check` in the root
`package.json`, and `release:check` is what .github/workflows/ci.yml and release.yml
run. So the rule does fire in CI. It is still the weaker of the two guarantees, because
it forbids an EDGE and rule 1 parses the import.
THE NUMBERS ARE A FLAT COUNTER AND NOTHING ELSE. The next code is the highest number in
`codes` and `retired` together, plus one; 0000 is unused because a code of all zeros reads
as `no code`. There are no per-package blocks and there must not be: a code is a PERMANENT
PUBLIC IDENTIFIER that outlives the console log it was printed in, and blocks tie it to an
INTERNAL layout that this repository moves — refusals move between files and functions,
packages are added (@exodra/term), packages exist with no block anybody remembered to
assign. Under blocks a refusal that changed package had two exits, failing the build or
renumbering, and renumbering is the one thing a permanent identifier may never do. `pkg` is
therefore a PLAIN FIELD for the reader: a refusal that moves package edits that field and
keeps its number. What the number costs by not being blocked is that it no longer says
which package spoke before you look it up — which the page tells you in its first line.
A NUMBER IS NEVER REUSED, AND `retired` IS WHAT MAKES THAT TRUE. Deleting a refusal does
not free its number: move the row into `retired`, where it keeps the number spoken for and
is exempt from the every-registered-code-is-thrown rule. The gate fails if a retired number
is thrown or registered again, and it fails on a GAP in the numbering — which is what stops
the evidence being erased instead of retired.
TWO FORMS, AND `payload` IS WHICH ONE A ROW USES. The bare form throws the code alone. The
appended form throws the code, one space, and NAMES ONLY — no verbs, no explanation, so it
cannot grow back into the sentence it replaced:
: 'EXO0001'                            bare
: `EXO0002 "${event}"`                 appended
Take the bare form when every name in the refusal is readable from the call the author
wrote, so that re-running that code in a development build reproduces the full sentence.
Take the appended form when the refusal names something the program can ASSEMBLE FROM DATA
— a pack built from a config, a composition built from a plugin registry — because then the
developer's run of 'the same code' is not the same code, and nothing on the user's console
says which name it was. A row with a `payload` must be thrown in the appended form and a
row without one in the bare form; the gate checks both directions.
Every field is required and the gate says so. `meaning` is the one sentence that says what
happened; `explanation` is what to do about it and why it is refused; `payload`, where a
row has one, says what follows the code. All of them are copied VERBATIM onto
docs-site/docs/errors.md, and the gate compares them — the registry is the source, the page
is the rendering, and they cannot drift into saying different things.
The FILE AND LINE a code is thrown from is deliberately not stored here. It would be stale
the first time somebody moved a function, and the gate finds the site by scanning instead.

what: THE ONE PLACE THE BYTE FIGURES ARE STATED. They used to be copied into three files with
nothing checking them, and they had already stopped reconciling. Every other file that
mentions the saving now cites this block by name, and
`packages/core/src/tests/errorCodeRegistry.test.ts` fails if any figure below reappears
measurement.how: A fresh `npm run build:all`, then the gzipped size of each package's built `dist/index.js`. THIS SENTENCE USED TO CLAIM IT WAS "the same measurement `scripts/check-bundle-size.mjs` reports", and it is not: that gate gzips `dist/exodra.esm.js`, the minified browser ESM a page actually loads, and the only thing it compares about `dist/index.js` is comment-stripped RAW bytes. So the figures below are not the gate's figures and have never been re-taken against it.
measurement.unit: gzipped bytes of the built package

superseded.said: That emptying every refusal message removed 2858 gzipped bytes from @exodra/dom, called 16.2% of the package, and 1536 from @exodra/core, called 30% of it. These are the numbers that started this work and they are the ones that were copied into three files.
superseded.status: SUPERSEDED AND UNMEASURED — do not quote them as current and do not rescale them. They came from an earlier build, and the percentages beside them were taken against that build's totals rather than the ones above. Nobody has re-run the emptied-message experiment against the build the `date` field above records, so the honest statement is that the saving was worth taking on the evidence of the day and has not been re-measured since. A percentage recomputed from two numbers measured on different days is a number nobody measured.

codes.payload: the name of the event port that was refused, in double quotes.
codes.meaning: A schema declares an event port for a name that the delegated event pack rendering it does not listen for.
codes.explanation: A delegated pack is built from a fixed list of event names and installs one listener per name on the render root. A port whose name is not in that list has nothing to dispatch it, so its handler could never fire and the element would be a button that does nothing. Add the event name to the createExoDelegatedEvents call that built the pack, or render this schema with a pack that covers it. The event name ships because a pack can be assembled from data — a config, a plugin registry, a list a host application composes — which is the same reason this check is not stripped in the first place; what a development build adds is the pack's whole list and the way out.

codes.payload: the tag of the child element that was declared and the tag of the element it was declared inside, in that order, each in double quotes.
codes.meaning: A schema declares a child element inside an element whose content is text, where no parser will ever read it back as an element.
codes.explanation: The refusal comes from ExoSchemaBuilder.el(), at schema-build time, and the parent is one of two lists. RAW TEXT is script, style, xmp, iframe, noembed, noframes, noscript and plaintext; RCDATA is textarea and title. No TAG is recognised between the tags of either kind, so the child would be characters there and not an element: the server prints the markup and a browser reading those same bytes builds one TEXT node, which is why the DOM backend — the side that parses its own output back — refuses the schema while the server happily serves it. One schema, two pages. If the child is content, move it OUT of that element. If it is meant to BE the text of the element, declare it with text(), which both backends emit verbatim in raw text and escape identically in RCDATA; in a raw-text element you may instead give the element a children port of its own, which is the unsafeHtml hatch and your boundary to hold. The two tags ship because a tag can be assembled from data — a schema a compiler emits over a template, an el() whose tag came from a component's own input, a builder adding kids in a loop over a config — so the developer's run of the same program may declare something else entirely; what a development build adds is the sentence, the markup both backends would have produced, and the way out.

codes.payload: the tag of the element the port was declared in, in double quotes, followed by the number of children already declared before the port.
codes.meaning: A schema declares a children port inside an element whose content is text, and that port is not the element's only child.
codes.explanation: The refusal comes from ExoSchemaBuilder.childrenPort(), at schema-build time, and the element is one of two lists. RAW TEXT is script, style, xmp, iframe, noembed, noframes, noscript and plaintext; RCDATA is textarea and title. A port in one of these is allowed on purpose — it is the documented way to put raw content in a script or a style — but only when it is the element's ONLY child, which is the same condition the string backend calls ownsElement. A port that shares its element has no filler left that both works and agrees: raw markup (set, bind) already throws on both backends, because a browser writes markup with innerHTML and that would destroy the siblings, and a nested instance diverges, printed as markup into the text by the server where no parser will read it back while the browser inserts real element nodes. In raw text a static in front of the port is also how a closing sequence gets spelled across the two halves and ends the element on the served page. Give the raw content a port that is the element's only child and put the static text INSIDE the value, or move the nested instance out of the element entirely. The tag and the count ship because a schema can be assembled from data — an element that gets a static base only when a theme is configured, and a port either way, has a development copy with one child and a deployed copy with two — so the count is the fact the developer's own run does not reproduce.

codes.meaning: A schema builder both named a port where it stands and returned a record of ports, and those are two spellings of one thing.
codes.explanation: The returned record is what the wiring factory reads, so every named port missing from that record would be unreachable: filled by nobody, with no error anywhere. The two spellings are refused rather than merged, because a name declared on both sides would need a winner and either answer silently drops a port the author wrote. Name each port where it stands and return nothing, or name none of them and return the record. A development build names the first port that was declared both ways.

codes.meaning: A schema builder finished without declaring a single element, so the schema has no root to render.
codes.explanation: Every backend reads the schema's first child as its root element, and a builder that declared only text, only a port, or nothing at all, leaves that slot empty. This refusal is not stripped from a production build although the fact it checks is as fixed as the multi-root one beside it: it is also the type narrowing that makes the root an element for everything downstream, and behind a guard it would need a cast asserting exactly what the check verifies. Declare one element with el() and put everything else inside it.

codes.meaning: A schema declares static text inside a plaintext element that spells a closing sequence for it, and nothing closes a plaintext.
codes.explanation: plaintext is the one element on the RAW TEXT list that runs to the END OF THE FILE, so those characters are text, and so is the closing tag the compiler writes after them. It is refused because the string is the one place an author says out loud that they expect the element to close, and it does not: every plaintext in a schema already prints bytes that no parser reads back as the tree that produced them, since the whole rest of the document becomes this element's text. Use pre, whose text both backends escape and which ends where it is written. A development build prints the sequence found, its offset, and the start of the run it was found in.

codes.meaning: A schema declares static text inside a raw text element that contains the closing sequence of that element.
codes.explanation: The text of a raw text element is written LITERALLY by both backends, because a character reference in there reaches the source as its own characters and HTML gives raw text no escape mechanism at all. So this text ends the element where it stands, and the rest of the schema is parsed as markup after it. Break the sequence across the expression that produces it, or give the element a children port of its own, which is the unsafeHtml hatch and your boundary to hold. A development build prints the sequence found, its offset, and the start of the adjacent run of static text it was found in, which is the unit checked because both compilers merge adjacent statics before emitting them.

codes.meaning: A schema declares static script text whose closing sequence is inert because an earlier unclosed comment armed the double escaped state, and it is refused anyway.
codes.explanation: This is a deliberate refusal of a run that works as written. An earlier unclosed opening comment plus script start has already put the tokenizer into the SCRIPT DATA DOUBLE ESCAPED state, where the closing sequence in this text closes nothing. It is kept because accepting a closing script sequence inside a script would rest the whole element boundary on this package's own tokenizer, which is a far larger claim than refusing one string. Break the CLOSING sequence to get past it, and not the opening one instead, which would leave that same closing sequence in the merely ESCAPED state where it really does end the element. A development build prints the sequence, its offset and the start of the run.

codes.meaning: A schema declares static script text that enters the tokenizer's script data double escaped state and never leaves it before the text ends.
codes.explanation: An unclosed opening comment earlier in this text put the tokenizer into script data ESCAPED, where a following script start tag plus a space, a slash or a greater-than arms the DOUBLE escaped state. In that state a closing script sequence does not emit an end tag at all: it only walks back one level. So the end tag the compiler writes after this text closes nothing, and every byte of the document after it is consumed as JavaScript source, which is a whole-page takeover from a run that contains no closing sequence at all. Close the comment before the end of the text, or break the script start so the tokenizer never sees it, or give the element a children port of its own, which is the unsafeHtml hatch and your boundary to hold. A development build prints the sequence that armed the state, its offset, and the start of the run.

codes.meaning: A schema declares a text port inside a raw text element, where the two backends cannot write the same bytes.
codes.explanation: The server escapes a text value and the HTML serialiser does not escape text in these elements, so the two would print different bytes, and the escaped one is broken anyway: a raw text element decodes no character references, so an escaped less-than reaches the source as those four characters. Writing it raw instead is not a fix either, because nothing can escape the closing sequence and a value carrying one would end the element and ship markup of its own. If the content is genuinely raw, give the element a children port of its own, which is the unsafeHtml hatch, and own the escaping there. A development build names the element.

codes.payload: the element name that was refused, in double quotes.
codes.meaning: A schema declares an element whose tag is not a legal element name.
codes.explanation: A tag reaches the markup VERBATIM on every backend and cannot be escaped, since an escaped tag is not a tag. So a name carrying a greater-than, a space or a quote does not make an oddly-named element, it makes MARKUP, and a name that closes the tag and opens an img with an onerror ships a working handler from the server AND in the browser. Legal is narrower than HTML's own custom-element rule on purpose: a letter, then letters, digits or hyphens, which covers div, svg, feGaussianBlur and my-widget. The name ships with the code because a tag can be assembled from data, which is the bug this most often is; check it against the elements you mean to allow before it reaches el().

codes.meaning: A schema declares a value port on a select or an output element, and the server can print no attribute that carries it.
codes.explanation: Both compilers cut the markup exactly once per port, in numbering order, so a port's writer can only emit bytes at its own slot. For a select, the markup that says which option is chosen is selected on the OPTION, a different element and later in the document than this port's slot, so the server prints nothing and serves the FIRST option while the client render shows another: the wrong page until the bundle arrives, and forever with JavaScript off. Say it on the options instead, giving each option a selected port filled with whether the model equals that option's value, which also works when the options are a list. For an output, the value IS the text content and HTML gives it no value content attribute anywhere, so write the text with textPort() instead; an output is not user-editable, so its text is its value on both backends and nothing can drift.

codes.meaning: A schema names a port __proto__, which cannot be filed in the record a wiring function reads.
codes.explanation: The record is a plain object literal, so assigning __proto__ on it calls the inherited setter and REPLACES THE PROTOTYPE instead of filing the port. The port would not be in the record at all, the wire reading it would get whatever the prototype chain has, and nothing would throw. The name is fixed, so nothing is appended to the code. Give the port any other name.

codes.payload: the port name that was declared twice, in double quotes.
codes.meaning: A schema declares two ports with the same name, and the record a wiring function reads can hold only one of them.
codes.explanation: The record is one object, so the second declaration is an assignment over the first and the losing port becomes unreachable: still numbered, still compiled, filled by nothing, and nothing thrown. The type layer cannot catch it, because a key is a key however many calls claim it. Names are per SCHEMA and not per element, so two elements declaring the same thing still need two names. The name ships with the code because a port name can be assembled from data, so the developer's own run is not the run that decides it.

codes.meaning: A connector call that fills children was handed a port that is not a children port.
codes.explanation: A children fill needs a place in the tree to put instances in. A text port's value is written as TEXT, escaped into the markup on the server and set as text in the browser, and an attribute port is not a place in the tree at all, so neither can hold children. Declare the position with childrenPort() where the children stand, and fill that port instead. A development build names the backend and the method that was called.

codes.meaning: A component built with createExoStatic declared ports, and a static component has no wiring to fill them.
codes.explanation: A static component arms nothing at all, so those ports would stay empty for the life of the page with no error anywhere. Build a machine with createExoMachine and fill them with withExoWire, or drop the ports. A development build prints how many ports the schema declared.

codes.meaning: A schema spells an attribute className, and this renderer writes the name the markup actually carries.
codes.explanation: React spells it that way because class is a reserved word in a JSX property position. Here an attribute name is a plain string or an object key, so nothing stops you writing the name the markup carries, and accepting both spellings would make one attribute answer to two names for no gain. Write class.

codes.payload: the attribute name that was refused, in double quotes.
codes.meaning: A schema declares an attribute or a port whose name is not a legal attribute name.
codes.explanation: A name is written into the markup VERBATIM and cannot be escaped, because an escaped name is a different attribute. So a name carrying a quote, a space, an equals, a less-than or a greater-than does not produce an oddly-named attribute, it produces MARKUP: a name that closes the value and opens an onclick ships a working handler from the server AND in the browser, since both backends print the same bytes. Legal is an allowlist and not a blocklist, because the same string is also parsed as markup when the DOM plan is compiled: a letter or an underscore, then letters, digits, underscores, dots, colons, dollars or hyphens, which covers data-id, aria-label, class, viewBox and xlink:href. It throws rather than dropping the port, because a port that emitted nothing would still hold the port number both backends index their plans by, moving every later value onto the wrong element. The name ships with the code because it can come from data, which is the bug this usually is; build it from a fixed prefix and a value you have checked.

codes.payload: the tag of the element and the markup spelling they collide on, in that order, each in double quotes.
codes.meaning: A schema declares a port whose markup spelling is already carried by a static attribute on the same element.
codes.explanation: There is no element with two attributes of one name: the server would print both and a browser would keep the FIRST, while the DOM backend's setter would overwrite the static. The same schema, two different pages, and a hydration mismatch between them. It is refused rather than resolved, because the port wins is an artefact of fill order and stops being true the moment a wire skips the port. The comparison is between markup SPELLINGS and not raw names. Keep the port and give the default value to the wire, or drop the port and keep the static. The tag and the spelling ship with the code because either can be assembled from data.

codes.payload: the tag of the element and the markup spelling they collide on, in that order, each in double quotes.
codes.meaning: A schema declares two ports whose markup spellings are the same attribute on one element.
codes.explanation: The server prints both and a browser keeps the first, while the DOM backend has one attribute that both setters write, so the LAST fill wins: two different pages from one schema. Event ports are exempt from the comparison because they write no markup on any backend, so their names cannot collide with an attribute. Use one port and decide the value in the wire. The tag and the spelling ship with the code because either can be assembled from data.

codes.meaning: The createInitialState option of createExoMachine was handed a value instead of a function that makes one.
codes.explanation: This is the one place the shared-object bug can be caught. A value handed here would be ONE object shared by every instance of the component, each instance seeing every other instance's writes, and nothing downstream could tell that apart from intent. createInitialState takes a function so that each instance gets its own value. Wrap the value in a function that returns it.

codes.meaning: A schema being hydrated declares a port on a static element that stands between two children ports, where the adoption walk cannot reach that element.
codes.explanation: In a component shaped like h3, then child list a, then hr, then child list b, then footer, the hr is short by child list a's rows counted forward and by child list b's rows counted back, so this port would be wired onto one of a's list rows with nothing in the markup to show it. The child list BEHIND such a static is recovered from the one in FRONT of it when that one adopts; a port on the static itself cannot be, because a wiring function is free to fill it first. Give one of the two child lists its own element, or move the port off the separator. A client render of the same schema is unaffected: only adoption is refused, and the refusal is raised while the hydrate plan is compiled rather than while the DOM plan is.

codes.meaning: A page asked a DOM backend to hydrate and that backend was never composed with withExoHydration.
codes.explanation: Hydration is a plugin pack, not a built-in, so a backend that was not composed with it holds no adopting surface at all. Compose it once, at module level, as const backend = withExoHydration(new ExoDomBackend()), and render from the same object you hydrate with. Without this refusal the first c.set of an adopted page raises a TypeError on a method name from inside a compiled wire, which says nothing about hydration or about composition.

codes.meaning: A children port on a hydrating page was filled before the child list standing in front of it on the same element had been filled.
codes.explanation: Adoption is eager and reads the server's own nodes, so a child list standing behind another one only learns where its markup begins once the one in front has claimed its rows. Fill the children ports of one element in DOCUMENT ORDER, and fill every one of them, remembering that an empty list is a fill. A client render and the server accept any order; only adoption cannot, because no table can hold the landing of a list whose start depends on how many rows the previous list took.

codes.meaning: The walk that adopts a served page reached a position where the server's markup has no element at all.
codes.explanation: Hydration creates nothing, so the page was rendered from a different schema, a different wiring or different data than the one running here. Carrying on would wire the NEXT element as this instance, which puts data on the wrong line instead of raising an error. The site names what it was looking for as a constant string, because it runs once per adopted instance and must not allocate on the path that does not throw.

codes.meaning: A children port that shares its element with other children was filled with set on a page being hydrated.
codes.explanation: The only way to write raw markup is innerHTML, which would destroy the other children. Nested instances go through one, list or childList; raw markup, the unsafe html hatch, needs a port that is its element's ONLY child. The server and a client render refuse this same program by design, and the development message is split at the same place as the client render's so that one refused program is described one way wherever a developer meets it. It names no tag, unlike the client-side refusal, because a silenced port is retargeted to the instance root and the only tag reachable would be the wrong one.

codes.meaning: The server's markup at one position of a children port is not the element the child standing there was built from.
codes.explanation: The walk that wires an instance is compiled against the schema and inspects nothing, so it cannot be aimed at a different element. Either the page was served by a different build than the one running here, or the wiring function assembles its children in a different order from the one it places them in, and a hydrating build takes the server's elements in document order. The development message carries the shape checker's own account of the disagreement, of the expected span, found b kind; that is a sentence rather than a name, so it does not follow the code.

codes.meaning: A children port could not be reconciled on a server-rendered page because another children port stands directly behind it.
codes.explanation: While hydrating, a child list opens an adoption cursor over the rows the server printed and each build adopts the next one. That needs the list's end, and where another child list stands behind it with no static element between them, the first row of the one behind cannot be told from a surplus of this one. Put a static element between the two child lists, adopt with c.list(port, component, count), which is told how many rows to take, or render this component on the client instead of hydrating it.

codes.meaning: A node that was not made by createExoNode was placed in a children port.
codes.explanation: What arrives is a bare Element with no mount, no unmount and no disposers, so it carries no lifecycle of its own and a list cannot know when to end subscriptions it never made. Children placed in a children port must come from createExoNode. Without this check the page gets a DOM exception about insertBefore's first parameter from inside a diff, naming nothing. The message carries no runtime value, because the offending node is by definition not one of ours and there is nothing of it this function may read.

codes.meaning: A schema put a port among an element's attributes that has no name, where only attribute and event ports belong.
codes.explanation: The DOM plan writes an attribute by name, so a nameless port among the attributes has nothing to write to. The check is not strippable: it is what narrows the name to a string for the attribute writer. Declare the port with a name, or move it to where it belongs, which for content is a text port or a children port declared inside the element.

codes.meaning: A schema declares children or a content port inside a void element, which cannot hold either.
codes.explanation: The parser closes a void element itself and the serialiser prints no end tag, so anything inside it is reparented as a SIBLING. The string backend would print a closing tag and a browser re-parses that into a second element of the same name, so the two backends would serve different pages from one schema. Move the children to a container element.

codes.meaning: A schema gives one element both a content port and static children.
codes.explanation: A content port stands for EVERYTHING inside its element, so the static children vanish from the markup while their ports keep the indices this plan addresses by, and every setter after them is built against the wrong element. Move the static children into the wiring, or drop the port.

codes.meaning: Part of a schema whose root is SVG content broke out of the SVG when the prototype markup was parsed.
codes.explanation: The HTML parser closes foreign content the moment it meets an HTML tag it knows, among them div, p, table and span, and a browser does the same to the markup the server sends. Put HTML inside a foreignObject, which is the one element that may hold it. The development message also prints the first bytes of the markup the schema produced, so that the offending tag can be seen without rebuilding the schema by hand.

codes.meaning: A text port whose writer stores into a Text node has no Text node in the parsed prototype.
codes.explanation: The writer has nothing to store into, which means the parser reshaped this element. A text port emits a placeholder character into the prototype markup precisely so that a Text node exists to cache and mutate; a parse that dropped or merged it away leaves the writer addressing nothing. The development message prints the first bytes of the markup the schema produced.

codes.meaning: A port that the DOM plan can only address by name reached the compiler without one.
codes.explanation: The name is refused rather than coerced: the throw is what narrows it to a string for the writer built from it. A port declared with no name cannot be addressed as an attribute, a property or an event, so there is nothing for the plan to compile. Declare the port with the name it is meant to write.

codes.meaning: A children port that shares its element with other children was filled with set during a client render.
codes.explanation: The only way to write raw markup is innerHTML, which would destroy those other children. Nested instances go through one, list or childList; raw markup, the unsafe html hatch, needs a port that is its element's ONLY child. This refusal is what a children port's setter slot holds when the port shares its element, so that the slot is never empty and set is never a call on undefined; the hydrating twin of it is split at the same place on purpose.

codes.meaning: A subscription was made with neither an owning child nor an ambient teardown scope to end it.
codes.explanation: A subscription nothing can end is a leak that looks like it worked. A child beats the ambient scope whenever there is one, because a child can leave while its render goes on and its subscriptions must go with it, which is why the owner is passed down rather than read from the module. With neither owner available, wrap the render in exoTeardownScope and keep the disposer it returns.

codes.meaning: A ref port was filled with set or bind, and a ref port has no writer at all.
codes.explanation: A ref port exists ONLY so that a wire can obtain the element, to observe it, focus it or measure it, and that is what the connector's port node reader hands back. In TypeScript the call does not compile, so reaching it means the port arrived from untyped code. If the element needs a VALUE written to it, declare an attribute port, a text port or an event port beside this one: an element may carry as many ports as it likes. The refusal fills the setter slot rather than leaving a hole, because the table is typed and a hole would mean a guard on the hottest line in the package.

codes.payload: the name of the event port whose descriptor was filled, in double quotes.
codes.meaning: An event port was filled with an action descriptor and no subject, where the connector's on call takes port, action and subject.
codes.explanation: A descriptor names a property, which is what lets ONE descriptor serve every row; a descriptor that carried its own row would be a closure with extra steps. The subject is usually the row's item. It is refused when the port is FILLED and not when the user clicks, because left to dispatch a forgotten third argument surfaces as a button that throws in production, days later and far from the wire. The event name ships because a pack can be assembled from data, so the developer's own run need not reproduce it.

codes.payload: the name of the event the pack was asked to delegate, in double quotes.
codes.meaning: A delegated event pack was asked for an event name that does not bubble, so a listener on the render root would never see it.
codes.explanation: Every descriptor for that name would be dead. Use the bubbling twin where there is one, focusin and focusout for focus and blur, or leave the name out of this pack and let it keep the direct strategy. The check is asked when a schema's port is attached rather than when the pack is built, which refuses fewer working programs at the cost of never reporting a dead name in a pack's list. It is NOT stripped in production: the argument for stripping holds for a literal list written at module level and not for a pack assembled from DATA, a config or a plugin registry, where the name is not settled before the program ships. The name follows the code for that same reason.

codes.payload: the name of the high-frequency event the pack was asked to delegate, in double quotes.
codes.meaning: A delegated event pack was asked for a high-frequency event without the option that says the cost is intended.
codes.explanation: This is not the non-bubbling refusal: the event does bubble and delegating it WORKS. It is refused because of what it costs. The root's listener runs on every one of these, and each run walks from the event target up to the root reading one property per ancestor, at the pointer's sampling rate rather than when a person acts, for as long as the pointer is moving and whether or not anything on that path has a handler. Under the direct strategy the same stream reaches one listener on one element and stops. If a delegated high-frequency event is what you mean, a drag served by ONE listener on a root instead of one per row, say so in the call by passing allowHighFrequency true; otherwise leave the name out of this pack and let it keep the direct strategy. The name follows the code because a pack can be assembled from data.

codes.meaning: An element handed to the foreign-child door is already in a tree, so something else owns it.
codes.explanation: The first list that placed it would silently take it out of there. A foreign child must be an element nobody has placed yet: create it, or let the foreign renderer create it, and hand it in detached. If you really mean to take over markup that is already on the page, calling remove on the element first is what writes the theft down where it happens. A parent is the evidence here, and it is a HEURISTIC rather than a proof of ownership; the development message names the parent's tag.

codes.meaning: An element handed to the foreign-child door already carries an Exodra child lifecycle from an earlier call.
codes.explanation: Making a second one for it would leave the element and the list that holds it pointing at different objects. Keep the child that the first call returned and place that one. A child that leaves a list and comes back is moved, not re-adopted, so this is the narrow refusal of an element the door recognises in its own set rather than a judgement about where the element currently stands.

codes.meaning: A foreign child's mount hook moved the element out of the parent the list had put it in.
codes.explanation: Only removal climbs; every insertion and every anchor in the list addresses this element directly, so the next child inserted beside it would throw a DOM exception from inside a diff and leave the list half-applied. Render INTO the element instead of moving it, and if the foreign renderer needs a wrapper, pass the wrapper to the foreign-child door and let it render inside that.

codes.meaning: One foreign child is being placed while a list already holds it, which would put one element in two positions.
codes.explanation: One element cannot be in two places, and both lists would go on holding it: the first one to drop it runs your unmount hook on a widget that is still on screen in the other, and the second drop runs it again. Make one foreign node per position. What a caller holds is the foreign node, and holding it in two children ports, or twice in one array, is holding one element twice. It is refused at the SECOND placement, which is the first moment anything can tell.

codes.meaning: A children port that shares its element with other children was filled with set while rendering to a string.
codes.explanation: The DOM backend can only write raw markup with innerHTML, which would destroy those other children, so printing it here would render on the server and throw in the browser. Nested instances go through one, list or childList; raw markup, the unsafe html hatch, needs a port that is its element's ONLY child. The server refuses the same program its client twin does, which is what keeps one schema from having two meanings.

codes.meaning: A ref port was filled with set or bind while rendering to a string.
codes.explanation: A ref port has no writer on any backend. It exists only so that a wire can obtain the element, which is a browser-side capability and prints nothing on the server. Declare an attribute port or a text port if a value is meant to reach the markup.

codes.meaning: An attribute port reached the string backend's writer factory without a name.
codes.explanation: An attribute is printed by name, so a nameless attribute port has nothing to print. The throw is what narrows the name to a string for the writer built from it. Declare the port with the attribute name it is meant to write.

codes.meaning: A schema declares content or children inside a void element, and the string backend refuses to print it.
codes.explanation: The parser closes a void element for you and prints no end tag, so this backend would emit a closing tag and a browser would re-parse it into a SECOND element of the same name, while the DOM backend drops the content instead: one schema, two pages. Put the content in a sibling element. This check deliberately SHIPS while the other three guards in the same compiler stay stripped, because the other three compare two pieces of our own code walking one schema, where a user's machine cannot produce a disagreement the first local compile did not.

codes.meaning: A port was numbered by the schema and never reached by the terminal backend's plan compiler, and a wire then filled it.
codes.explanation: The two walks disagree about the shape of the schema, which means the plan holds no writer for that port. A gap read as undefined would instead throw that undefined is not a function from inside the connector's set, naming nothing, so the missing entry is filled with a refusal that says which port index is unaccounted for.

codes.meaning: A port carries an index outside the range of port numbers the schema declared.
codes.explanation: Either the schema was not closed, so its ports were never numbered, or the root handed to the compiler was not the numbered one. Everything in this backend is indexed by the port's own index, so an index outside the range would write past the end of the writer table.

codes.meaning: A schema declares content or children inside a void element, and the terminal backend refuses it.
codes.explanation: This backend has no parser and would happily hold the content, and it refuses anyway: a schema must be accepted or refused identically by every backend, or one schema means two things. The shared refusals are asked here even though nothing in a text tree needs them.

codes.meaning: A port of a kind other than a children port stands among an element's children.
codes.explanation: Only a children port belongs among an element's children; an attribute port or an event port belongs in the element's attributes, and a text port is declared as the element's content. The development message names the kind that was found.

codes.meaning: The connector's set was used on a port kind that has no value to write in a text tree.
codes.explanation: An event port is filled with the connector's on call; a children port is filled with one, list, childList or keyedList; a ref port is read through the port node reader rather than written at all. The development message names which of the three was refused and which call to use instead. The refusal fills the writer slot rather than leaving a hole, because the table has one entry per port.

codes.meaning: An attribute port reached the terminal backend's writer table without a name.
codes.explanation: An attribute is stored by name in this backend's attribute record, so a nameless attribute port has nothing to store under. Declare the port with the name it is meant to write.

codes.meaning: A port-writer table was asked for a port kind it holds no entry for.
codes.explanation: A backend or a plugin may supply its own port-writer table, and this backend looks a kind up in that table rather than running a chain of comparisons, so a kind the table does not answer is answerable without editing the package. A backend supplying its own table must answer every kind its schemas can hold. The development message names the kind that was asked for.

codes.meaning: A children port belonging to a different schema than the one being wired was handed to a fill call.
codes.explanation: A port may only be filled by the wire of the component whose schema declared it. A port is just an object with an index on it, so nothing in the shared surface can catch this by type; the instance catches it by finding no region at that index. The development message names the call and the port's index.

codes.meaning: An event port with no name was handed to the terminal backend's listener call.
codes.explanation: A listener is stored under the event's name, so a nameless event port cannot be listened for. Declare the port with the event name it is meant to answer to.

codes.meaning: A component asked for the router with injectExoRouter and nothing standing above it had provided one.
codes.explanation: Exodra router: nothing above this component provided a router. Call provideExoRouter(c, router) in the wiring of a component that stands above it — the root of the page is the ordinary place — and do it on the server as well as in the browser, since the same wire runs on both. The refusal happens where inject() would otherwise answer undefined, because with no router an outlet shows nothing and a link cannot resolve an href, and both of those would fail later with nothing naming the missing provide.

codes.meaning: createExoBrowserHistory was called where there is no window to read a location from and no history to push into.
codes.explanation: createExoBrowserHistory requires a browser window. It reads location.pathname, location.search and location.hash and it pushes through the History API, so with neither an options.window nor a global window there is nothing for it to be a history OF. This is the refusal a server render hits when the browser history is built at module scope: build it inside the browser entry, or pass the window explicitly, and give the server createExoMemoryHistory instead.

codes.meaning: A lazy route loader resolved to a module export that is not a page component, caught while a caller is still awaiting the preload.
codes.explanation: Exodra router: a lazy route resolved to something that is not a page component. A page is a machine — the value createExoMachine, or a decorator over it, returns — and the module this loader imported exports something else (the previous runtime's h() schema, or a module with no default). It is refused inside preloadExoPage, where a caller is awaiting and can see it, rather than inside a subscriber with no stack pointing at the route table.

codes.payload: the path of the route whose component was refused, in double quotes.
codes.meaning: A matched route carries a component that is neither a page nor a lazy loader, so the route boundary has nothing it can render.
codes.explanation: Exodra router: the route has a component the schema core cannot render. A page here is a machine — the value createExoMachine, or a decorator over it, returns — or an exoLazy() loader that resolves to one. The route path ships because a route table is routinely assembled from data — a config, a manifest, a per-tenant list — so the developer's own run may hold different routes entirely, and a bare code would name none of them.

codes.meaning: A component assembled by withExoComputedMachine declared its machine in a way the machine cannot hold, and the assembly is refused at wire-build time.
codes.explanation: This is the one code for every refusal withExoComputedMachine makes while assembling a component's machine, and a development build names which one: mounted() was declared twice where it is one field; or a field of this component is read by none of its derivations, fills and effects, so nothing could ever wake it and it is a field that is written and never observed. Both are structural mistakes in how the component was declared, so re-running the same module in development reproduces the same message word for word.

codes.meaning: A wiring block body returned without calling done(), leaving the block unarmed for the instance it was building.
codes.explanation: exoWiring: this wiring block never called done(). Call done() at the end of the body, after the last declaration. A block that never armed compiled nothing, filled nothing, and no transition of it can commit — every symptom is a component that renders empty and never moves, with nothing in the output pointing back at the missing call, which is why the block refuses here instead of letting the instance run.

codes.meaning: A wiring block declaration disagreed with the block's own rules or with what the first instance of the same component declared.
codes.explanation: This is the one code for every refusal an ExoWiringBlock makes, and a development build names which one. A block is closed once it arms, so anything declared after done() is refused, and done() itself may be called only once. Everything else is the same rule seen from a different side: every instance of a component must declare the same fields, derivations, fills and effects, in the same order, with the same read lists and the same kinds, because the first instance is what compiled the shared program and a later instance that declares something else has no slot to put it in. The refusals name the slot, what the first instance declared there and what this one declared instead — including mounted(), which is one field and must be declared in one place or in none. All of it is a property of the component's own code, so the same run in development reproduces the message exactly.

codes.meaning: A machine specification was rejected while compiling it into a program, at module load, before any instance exists.
codes.explanation: This is the one code for every refusal compileExoMachine makes, and everything is refused there — at module load — because a flat description has nowhere to put a run-time guard that would not be paid on every commit forever. A development build names which rule was broken: more enode fields than the ceiling; more derivations and bodies than share one pending word; a derivation reading a field past the number declared; a DERIVATION that reads nothing, so nothing could wake it (a BODY that reads nothing is accepted); a port still at -1, meaning the machine was compiled outside the wire factory that numbers ports; a store into a field past the number declared, or into one declared with no writer; and an order that is not topological, where a derivation stores a field that a derivation declared at or before it already reads. The message names the offending derivation and, for the ordering rule, every derivation that reads the field too early.

codes.meaning: A machine derivation was pointed at an event port or a ref port, neither of which a derivation is able to fill.
codes.explanation: withExoComputedMachine: a derivation cannot fill an EVENT port — use on(port, handler) inside withExoHandlers; and a derivation cannot fill a REF port — use portNodeReader() to READ the node. A derivation produces a value and stores it, which is what attribute, text and children ports accept. An event port is a place a handler is installed, not a place a value lands, and a ref port exists so the wire can read the node back out; filling either from a derivation has no meaning the backend could carry out.

codes.meaning: A machine field was numbered outside the range a single word of bits can address, refused where the number is written.
codes.explanation: exoFieldBit refuses a field index outside 0..EXO_MACHINE_LIMIT - 1. It is a checked spelling of 1 << index, so the ceiling is refused where the number is WRITTEN rather than at the first commit that quietly ran the wrong derivation: 1 << 31 is negative and 1 << 32 is 1, so a component past the cap would get a bit belonging to another field and wake something other than itself. A machine that needs more fields than the cap needs to be split into more than one machine.

codes.meaning: A bound transition was dispatched into before the wiring block it belongs to had armed, so there is no instance to apply it to.
codes.explanation: This transition fired before its wiring block armed; call done() at the end of the wire, before anything can dispatch into it. A bound transition applies its change to the block's instance and then settles it, and until done() runs there is no instance and no settler — so the alternative to refusing is a change written nowhere and a commit that never happens. Anything that can dispatch — an event handler, a subscription, a timer started in the body — has to be reachable only after the block arms.

codes.meaning: A JSX element reached the runtime jsx factory, which means the module carrying it was never put through the schema compiler.
codes.explanation: Exodra schema JSX reached the runtime, which means this module was never compiled. Add @exodra/babel-plugin-schema to the build (or babel-preset-exodra with mode: 'schema'): it replaces every exoJsx(…) with a module-level schema declaration, and there is no runtime here that could interpret an element. The factory exists at all so that a tsc emit resolves and fails with a sentence instead of a missing export; there is deliberately no Fragment export, because the compiler refuses one and an unresolved <></> is the honest end.

codes.meaning: A schema builder was used after the build that created it had finished. The builder is one cursor that moves, and a kept one points wherever the build left it.
codes.explanation: The builder is ONE object that walks down into each element and back up again, so a reference kept past the callback it was handed to stands wherever the cursor stopped, not where it was captured. After the build it stands in a schema whose ports are already numbered: the element would reach no plan and the port would be filled by nobody, with no error anywhere. Declare everything inside the build callback, and call fork() where two positions are genuinely needed at once.

codes.payload: the tag of the element whose callback the cursor was handed to, in double quotes.
codes.meaning: A schema cursor was written to after the element callback it was handed to had already returned. The builder is one cursor that moves, so it now stands somewhere else entirely.
codes.explanation: The builder walks down into each element and back up again, so a reference stashed in one element’s callback and used from a later one writes into whatever element the cursor stands on now, not the one it was captured in. The element or the port lands in the wrong parent, with no error anywhere. Declare everything inside the callback it belongs to, and call fork() where two positions are genuinely needed at once. This refusal exists only when withExoSchemaAsserts is composed in.

codes.meaning: withExoSchemaAsserts is not the outermost decorator on a schema, and the decorator composed outside it would see only the top-level calls.
codes.explanation: The asserting cursor hands every element callback a fresh guarded cursor of its own, which replaces on receiver whatever a decorator composed outside it put there. That outer decorator would then see the top-level calls and none of the nested ones, silently, and half a decorator is worse than none. Compose the asserts last: withExoSchemaAsserts(withYourOwnDecorator(cursor)).

codes.meaning: An event port was filled with set or bind, and a handler is not a value an event port holds.
codes.explanation: Use the connector's on call, on port handler subject, which reaches the events pack this composition chose; a handler stored as an attribute or as text would print the source of the function and never fire. In TypeScript this call does not compile, so reaching it means the port arrived from untyped code. The refusal fills the setter slot rather than leaving a hole, because on no longer reads that table at all: it calls the pack's attach with the port's datum, so the only thing that can arrive at the slot is a fill door that mistook an event port for a value port.

codes.meaning: createExoDomSchema was handed a JSON declaration whose port carries no name, and the kind it was written as needs one.
codes.explanation: An attribute port IS the attribute it names and an event port IS the event it names, so a JSON declaration that wrote one of those without a name describes nothing a writer could be chosen for. A JSON declaration comes out of exoDomJsonDeclaration, which reads the names off a compiled schema, so a nameless port here means the JSON declaration was written or edited by something other than that function.
codes.payload: which of the two kinds was missing its name.

codes.meaning: createExoDomSchema parsed the JSON declaration's markup and got no element back.
codes.explanation: A schema holds ONE root element — the compile that produced the JSON declaration refused anything else — so its markup must parse to exactly that. An empty string, a comment, bare text or a fragment of several roots all land here, and all of them mean the JSON declaration is not one exoDomJsonDeclaration produced.

codes.meaning: A machine whose declaration carries no DOM JSON form reached a backend that has no compiler composed into it.
codes.explanation: render under withExoBuiltSchemas, and one/list/build on any backend, turn a machine's declaration into a schema. With no compiler composed, the only way to do that is the JSON form a build writes onto the declaration, and this declaration has none. Either compose withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend()), or declare the component with exoJsx under @exodra/babel-plugin-schema, which compiles the declaration at build time and writes that form onto it.

codes.meaning: c.foreign(...) was called while hydrating on a backend that did not compose EXO_DOM_FOREIGN_VOCABULARY.
codes.explanation: foreign is a pack, not a door every backend answers. The hydrate pass hands the call to the backend's own foreign, so the backend the page hydrates through needs the pack as much as the one it renders through: compose EXO_DOM_FOREIGN_VOCABULARY onto it.

codes.meaning: withExoWire was handed a machine that already has a wire, and a machine holds exactly one wire.
codes.explanation: A machine has one wire: the transition the system runs after createInitialState and that can be run again with new params through wireExoNode. Two would leave it unclear which one a re-run calls, so put both bodies in one withExoWire.

codes.meaning: overrides() was handed a name that is not a transition of this machine.
codes.explanation: An override table is indexed by the position withExoTransitions gives each name it declares, so only a name declared by withExoTransitions on this machine, or on a machine it was composed from, can be overridden. Declare the transition with withExoTransitions first, or call overrides() on the machine that declared it.

codes.meaning: c.one or c.list was called from a wire that wireExoNode re-ran on a live instance.
codes.explanation: c.one and c.list place their children once, while the instance is armed, so a second call would stack a second set beside the first. Call them in createInitialState, or place children with the children port methods (createExoNode, appendChild, insertChild, moveChild, removeChild), which any wire, transition or effect may call at any time.

codes.meaning: nextExoId was called where nothing above the component called provideExoIds.
codes.explanation: Ids are counted per render, so the counter has to be created by the render itself: call provideExoIds(c, prefix) in the createInitialState of the root, on the server and in the browser, and every nextExoId below it counts from the same start on both sides.

codes.payload: the number of roots the cursor produced.
codes.meaning: A schema's markup function produced more than one root element.
codes.explanation: A schema is ONE element: every root after the first would be dropped from the markup and its ports would keep the -1 they start with. Put siblings inside the root, with a children port where a run of children stands, or make each top-level element its own component.

codes.meaning: A schema's markup function minted a different kind of port at a position than it did when its ports were numbered.
codes.explanation: Port numbers are handed out in call order, so a markup function must make the same calls in the same order every time it runs. A branch that declares an attribute port on one run and a text port on another hands the wiring a number that means something else.

codes.meaning: exoPorts was given a declaration whose value is not one of the seven port kinds.
codes.explanation: exoPorts numbers ports in declaration order and mints each one from its kind mark, so every value in the declaration has to be one of EXO_PORT_ATTR, EXO_PORT_ATTR_STRING, EXO_PORT_ATTR_TOGGLE, EXO_PORT_TEXT, EXO_PORT_CHILDREN, EXO_PORT_EVENT or EXO_PORT_REF. Anything else would mint a port the wiring cannot write to.

codes.payload: the tag or namespace that was refused, in double quotes.
codes.meaning: A schema contains SVG or MathML markup and the DOM backend rendering it was composed without withExoForeignNamespaces.
codes.explanation: The SVG and MathML tables — tag and attribute case adjustment, namespaced attributes, HTML integration points — are a pack, so a page with no SVG links none of them. Compose withExoForeignNamespaces once, at module level, on the backend that renders a schema with svg, math or an SVG-only element in it.

codes.payload: the namespace of the element whose attribute was refused, in double quotes.
codes.meaning: A schema built from a JSON declaration has an attribute on an SVG or MathML element, and the backend was composed without withExoForeignNamespaces.
codes.explanation: createExoDomSchema decides which attribute a port writes from the element's namespace, and the SVG and MathML attribute tables are a pack. Compose withExoForeignNamespaces on the backend that builds a schema with SVG or MathML in it.

codes.payload: the index of the event port that already had a handler.
codes.meaning: A machine registered a second handler on an event port that already had one.
codes.explanation: An element keeps one handler per event: both events packs store it in one field, so a second registration on the same port would silently replace the first. Handle the port once — a handler can do several things — and keep it in one withExoHandlers step or one plugin step, not both.

codes.payload: the name.
codes.meaning: withExoEffects was given a dictionary with a name that is already taken on the machine's effects array.
codes.explanation: The dictionary form sets each effect's handle on the effects array under its name, so the name must be free there: a second withExoEffects step that repeats a name would leave two effects and reach only the newer one by name, and a name such as push, slice or length would shadow the array member the next step copies with. A name made of digits is refused as well, because it would write an element of the array instead of a name on it. Pick another name.

codes.payload: the name.
codes.meaning: withExoTransitions was given a name the machine already has as a transition, or a name that is an array index.
codes.explanation: A later step that repeats a name would leave two wrappers: a step that already destructured m.transitions keeps calling the first, and overrides() reaches only the first slot, so an override of the name would silently miss the newer one. A name made of digits is refused because object keys that look like indices change their order, and the override table is laid out by order. Give the transition its own name.

codes.meaning: A children port filled by c.one or c.list was given to a children port method or a reconciler.
codes.explanation: c.one and c.list place their children past the port's child list, so a port method or a reconciler on the same port would count none of them and insert in the wrong place. Place those children with createExoNode and appendChild / insertChild (or a reconciler) instead, or keep the hand-placed ones in a separate children port.

retired.note: A plugin declared a need for a plugin slot that no plugin in the composition provided. The named-slot runtime it belonged to was deleted: a backend is now an object that holds each plugin interface in a plain field, so an unprovided name is a missing method at compile time, not a boot refusal.

An application asked a composed runtime for a plugin slot that no plugin provided. Retired with EXO0001 and for the same reason: there is no runtime to ask, and reaching a plugin's API is a property read the checker verifies.

A connector's on() was handed a port that is not an event port. Every backend's on() now names TExoEventPort, whose kind field is a single numeric literal disjoint from the other four, so a text, attribute or children port is a compile error at the call and the runtime compare had nothing left to catch. It was deleted rather than left standing because on() runs once per event port per instance and the compare was measured on the events-build axis of packages/benchmarks; what refuses the mistake now is packages/type-tests/src/CARD.ts, where the wrong kind is offered to on() and rejected.

A machine was given a keep, an effect or a handler after done() had compiled it. Retired with the machine builder: createExoMachine and the decorators withExoTransitions, withExoWire, withExoHandlers and withExoEffects each return a new machine and leave their input unchanged, so there is no compiled machine for a late declaration to miss.
A machine builder's done() was called a second time. Retired with the machine builder: a machine is the value createExoMachine or a decorator returns, and there is no compile step to run twice.

attachExoKeyedList refused the same key twice while reconciling one children port. The keyed list is now createExoKeyedList in @exodra/list-reconcile (c.keyedList through EXO_KEYED_LIST_VOCABULARY), and the reconcileExoOrder pass under it gives each occurrence of a repeated key its own row, so a repeated key is two rows rather than an error.

A schema built its prototype by emitting markup and parsing it, so a markup string that parsed into anything but exactly one root was a refusal. The DOM plan compiler now builds the prototype by construction — createElement, createTextNode, appendChild — from a schema that is already a tree, so there is one root because one root is what was made.

An SVG-rooted schema used to be parsed inside a throwaway svg element and its namespace checked afterwards. The compiler now creates SVG and MathML elements with createElementNS directly, so the namespace is chosen rather than discovered and cannot come back wrong.

The walk compiled from a schema was replayed over the parsed prototype to prove the parser had not reshaped it. There is no parser on this path any more: the walk and the prototype come out of one construction pass, so the walk cannot run off a tree it built itself.

The compiled plan expected one tag where the parsed prototype had another — the parser having moved a tr out of a tbody and the like. Those reshapes are now refused at DECLARATION by assertExoParserStableChild.ts, which names the case instead of discovering it after the fact.

The variableName given to the hydration script renderer was not a dotted identifier path. Retired with renderExoHydrationScript, the renderer that assigned state to a global by that name: state now ships only as the JSON script renderExoPage() returns as page.stateScript, read with readExoStateScript(), and an element id is quoted data rather than source.

Two different observables were registered with the persistor under one key. Retired with the persistor and @exodra/reactivity: server state is written with c.inject(EXO_SSR_RESPONSE).setState(key, value) under keys the page chooses, and read back on the client with readExoStateScript(), so there is no registration to collide.

getExoPersistor was called while a server render was in progress. Retired with the process-wide persistor and @exodra/reactivity: a render's state lives on the response that render owns, reached through c.inject(EXO_SSR_RESPONSE), so there is no process-wide registry left to hand out.

mergeAttrs was called on @exodra/attrs, a tombstone that only threw. Retired with the package itself: it was deleted, because a package kept only so an old import resolves is the compatibility shim this project does not keep.

A machine declared its initial state twice. Retired when createInitialState moved into the options object of createExoMachine: an object literal has one createInitialState key, so a second declaration cannot be written.

A fill door was handed a port of a kind it does not fill, such as an attribute port handed to the call that places children. Retired with @exodra/wire and its withExoWiringAsserts decorator, which never shipped.

A fill door was handed a port that the schema being wired never declared, so its number addresses somebody else's table slot. Retired with @exodra/wire and its withExoWiringAsserts decorator, which never shipped.
One port was filled twice in a single wire, and only one of the two values can reach the page. Retired with @exodra/wire and its withExoWiringAsserts decorator, which never shipped.

A wire returned leaving ports that it declared and nobody filled, which is reported at the end because until then not yet and never are the same state. Retired with @exodra/wire and its withExoWiringAsserts decorator, which never shipped.

childList() was handed a port that is not a children port. Retired because the refusal is no longer dom's: @exodra/string grew the same door and accepted an attribute port in silence, writing a list's markup into an attribute slot, so both backends now raise core's assertExoChildrenPort (EXO0018) and there is one sentence for one mistake instead of two codes.

exoRouteMatchAt was asked for a match no route boundary had filed. Retired with exoRouteMatchAt itself: a page now receives its match as the params of its wire, and createInitialState receives it as its params, so there is no side table to miss.

A schema declared static text immediately after a children port. Retired when the DOM compiler learned to anchor the region on that Text node, and to put an empty comment before it where the server's parser would otherwise merge it into the text before the region or eat its newline; the string compiler prints the same comment, so both backends build one tree.

A machine placed children on a DOM backend composed without withExoChildList. Retired when the children port methods moved into every DOM backend: withExoChildList is now a deprecated call that returns its backend unchanged, so there is no composition left that lacks them.
